rv.q: Wilkinson's writing is wonderful and unique.
Night City may or may not be a 'choreopoem', but whatever you want to call it, it's a fine piece of new writing and deserves to have a big audience.
The real political strength of this show is in its seamless marriage of policy and its impact on people's actual lives.
While the three main threads don’t exactly coalesce into a fully integrated whole, there is a genuine sense that the playwright has worked to weave them.

As the allotted time she spends on each visit is cut, Tamara struggles to care for her patients: tellingly, her new boss refers to them as ‘customers.’ In one of the show’s few coincidences, Tamara is tasked with caring for her boss’s elderly mother, who hasn’t left her house in years. The three actors also play a range of other characters, too.
This paean to the mass of gig workers who slave in precarity to make London buzz 24/7 is timely, personal, and a battle-cry with nuance: not easy to bring off.
It's a thrilling ride as scenes flick and segue on a head-twist.
The production has a strong and committed ensemble, creating a vivid portrait of a city that never stops moving.
It rewards attention and offers something fresh to the debate, and some overfamiliar stories.
Whilst it didn't completely connect with me personally, there is a lot to appreciate in this intimate and engaging production, with three strong performances at its centre.

Night City paints a picture of an unsustainable work culture and the chains that bind people, but it tries to cover too much in too little time which dilutes the power of what could have been a sharper, more resonant exploration of the gig economy.
Overall, Night City feels messy, with too many characters, short scenes and not enough depth.
It is a hugely impressive play which deserves to fill the Little to the brim for its run – and a longer life somewhere too.

All three are doing work they have chosen, and have the capacity to succeed in. Jack initially loves the freedom and flexibility of working within the gig economy. But, as Night City shows us, it's good when it's good, but really bad when it's bad.

cn.t: Critics find this gig economy drama timely and well-intentioned, praising its authentic portrayal of London's precarious workers, but many feel the plotting becomes overly melodramatic and struggles to balance its ambitious social themes.
